Modern Slavery Act 2015, section 54 duty to publish a slavery and human trafficking statement - enforcement: NOT_FOUND as a criminal offence; the evidence shows it is not criminal — "The duties imposed on commercial organisations by this section are enforceable by the Secretary of State bringing civil proceedings in the High Court for an injunction or, in Scotland, for specific performance of a statutory duty under section 45 of the Court of Session Act 1988" [1].
Bribery Act 2010 offence of failing to prevent bribery - whether criminal and how punished: NOT_FOUND.

The Modern Slavery Act statement duty is not a criminal offence; it is enforced civilly by the Secretary of State through injunction or specific performance proceedings. The Bribery Act 2010 is not covered in the provided evidence, so its criminal nature and punishment cannot be confirmed here.

Yes, the Act reaches this conduct, under section 6 (bribery of foreign public officials).

- Section 6(1) makes it an offence for a person ("P") to bribe a foreign public official ("F") with the intention of influencing F in F's capacity as a foreign public official [5].
- Section 6(2) requires that P also intends to obtain or retain business or an advantage in the conduct of business — here, winning a government contract [5].
- Section 6(5)(a) defines a "foreign public official" as an individual holding a legislative, administrative or judicial position of a country outside the United Kingdom, which covers an official of a French ministry [6].
- Section 6(3) applies because F is neither permitted nor required by the applicable written law to be influenced by the payment [5].
- Territorially, section 12(1) does not apply since no act or omission took place in the UK, but section 12(2)–(3) extends jurisdiction where no act or omission forming part of an offence under section 1, 2 or 6 takes place in the UK, provided the person's acts done outside the UK would form part of the offence if done in the UK and the person has a close connection with the UK [10].
- Section 12(4) provides that a person has a close connection with the UK if, among other things, they were a British citizen at the time of the acts or omissions [1], and in such a case proceedings may be taken at any place in the United Kingdom [1].
